title: Replication
subtitle: Copies of the database — what they buy, and what they charge
objectives: Explain what replication scales and what it doesn't
Describe single-leader replication and the synchronous/asynchronous choice
Recognize replication lag bugs and the routing fixes for them
Reason about failover: lost writes, split brain, and choosing which mistake to make

exercises.prompt: Your app does 100 reads for every write, and your single database is drowning in reads. What's the structural fix?
choices: Add copies (replicas) that serve reads, leaving the original to handle writes
exercises.why: Reads can be served from any copy. Adding read replicas multiplies your read capacity without changing how writes work at all.
exercises.goDeeper: This only pays off because reads outnumber writes so heavily — which, happily, is true of most applications. The read:write ratio is the first number to establish before proposing replication: at 100:1 it's transformative, at 1:1 it buys you almost nothing.

exercises.prompt: The second reason to keep copies: your database machine dies at 3am. What does having a replica let you do?
choices: Nothing — you still restore from backup
Promote a replica to take over, so you stay online instead of waiting on a restore
Recover data faster from the dead disk
exercises.why: A replica is already running and already has (nearly) all the data. Promoting it takes seconds; restoring a backup takes hours.
exercises.goDeeper: Backups and replicas solve different problems and don't substitute for each other. A replica protects you from a machine dying. A backup protects you from someone running DELETE without a WHERE clause — because a replica would have faithfully replicated that too, instantly.

exercises.prompt: What does replication actually buy you? Select all.
choices: Serving users from a geographically closer copy
exercises.why: Reads, survival, and locality — yes. Write capacity — no: every write still has to be applied on every copy, so copies never reduce the write load.
exercises.goDeeper: That asymmetry is the most important fact about replication, and it's the reason sharding exists as a separate idea. If your bottleneck is writes, adding replicas makes things slightly worse, not better — you've added machines that all have to do every write, and none that do fewer.

exercises.prompt: Replication scales ______; it does nothing for write capacity.
exercises.why: Any copy can answer a read. Every copy must perform every write.

exercises.prompt: The moment you have two copies of the database, what have you inherited?
choices: The copies can disagree, so you now own a consistency problem
exercises.why: One copy can't disagree with itself. Two can drift apart — and now you must decide what happens when a reader lands on the copy that's behind.
exercises.goDeeper: This is unit 5's rule — every copy costs you a consistency question — arriving at industrial scale. Everything difficult in the rest of this unit is that one bill being itemized.

exercises.prompt: When is replication the WRONG tool for your scaling problem?
choices: When you have lots of reads
When writes are your bottleneck, or your dataset no longer fits on one machine
When users are spread across regions
exercises.why: Replication addresses read volume and machine failure. It doesn't reduce write load, and it doesn't make the data smaller — every copy holds the whole dataset.
exercises.goDeeper: Both of those limits point at the same successor idea: splitting the data across machines rather than duplicating it. That's sharding, and it's the other half of the scaling story.

exercises.prompt: Suppose any copy could accept writes. What breaks?
choices: Two copies could accept conflicting writes to the same row, and there'd be no single right answer
The copies would run out of disk
exercises.why: Two writers, one row, two different values — and nothing to arbitrate between them. Someone has to be the authority.
exercises.goDeeper: Which is why the standard design nominates exactly one copy to accept writes: the leader. Single-leader replication is the default in Postgres, MySQL, and most systems precisely because it dodges write conflicts by construction — with one writer, there is nothing to conflict.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of single-leader replication to its role.

pairs.right: The only copy that accepts writes
A read-only copy kept in sync
The stream of changes the leader ships
Promoting a follower when the leader dies

exercises.why: One writer, many readers, a stream of changes between them, and a plan for when the writer dies.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice the shape: the leader is a single point of failure for WRITES, but not for reads. That asymmetry drives everything in lesson 4 — losing the leader is an emergency, losing a follower is a Tuesday.

exercises.prompt: How does a follower stay in sync with the leader?
choices: The leader ships its stream of changes — its log — and the follower applies them in the same order
It copies the database files every night
exercises.why: The leader sends an ordered stream of changes; the follower replays them in that exact order, arriving at the same state.
exercises.goDeeper: That's the write-ahead log from unit 6, doing a second job. It exists for crash recovery — but an ordered record of every change turns out to be exactly what you'd want to ship to another machine. Replication rides on a log the database already had to write anyway.

exercises.prompt: Order a write under asynchronous single-leader replication.
steps: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader records the change in its log
Followers stream the log and apply the change
Followers can now serve the new data
exercises.why: Under asynchronous replication the leader answers the client before the followers have caught up — the client's write is done while the copies are still catching up.
exercises.goDeeper: Look closely at step 3 landing before step 4. That ordering is the entire source of the next two lessons: it's why followers can be stale, and why a leader dying at exactly that moment can lose a write it already called successful.

exercises.prompt: The leader can wait for a follower to confirm before telling the client 'done' (synchronous), or reply immediately and let followers catch up (asynchronous). What does synchronous buy and cost?
choices: It's faster and safer — strictly better
The write exists on two machines before you're told it succeeded — but every write now waits for the follower, and if that follower is down, writes stall
It buys nothing; it's a legacy option
exercises.why: You're buying the guarantee that an acknowledged write exists in two places, and paying for it with latency on every write plus a dependency on the follower being alive.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why fully synchronous replication to ALL followers is rare — one slow or dead follower would halt every write in the system. The usual compromise is semi-synchronous: one follower synchronous so a second copy always exists, the rest asynchronous so they can lag without blocking anyone.

exercises.prompt: Why is single-leader replication so common, despite the leader being a bottleneck for writes?
choices: Because having exactly one writer removes write conflicts entirely — a huge simplification for a cost most apps can afford
It's the only design that exists
exercises.why: It trades write scalability — which most apps don't need — for the elimination of an entire category of problem. That's usually a superb deal.
exercises.goDeeper: Keep this pattern in view: a huge amount of system design is buying simplicity with a constraint you can afford. One writer is a real limit, and it's also why you never have to answer 'which of these two conflicting values is correct?'

exercises.prompt: A user updates their profile (write goes to the leader), the page reloads, and the read is served by a follower that hasn't caught up yet. What do they see?
choices: Their OLD profile — their own change appears to have vanished
exercises.why: The follower is behind, so it answers with the state from before their write. The user's own change seems not to have saved.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the most common replication bug there is, and it's maddening because it only reproduces under load — when lag is large enough to notice. The fix is read-your-writes routing: for a short window after a user writes, send THAT user's reads to the leader.

exercises.prompt: The delay between a write landing on the leader and appearing on a follower is called replication ______.
exercises.why: Replication lag is the size of the window in which followers are answering with the past.

exercises.prompt: A user refreshes twice. The first read hits a caught-up follower and shows a new comment. The second hits a lagging follower and the comment is gone. What broke?
choices: Monotonic reads — for that user, time appeared to run backwards
exercises.why: Two reads, two replicas, two different amounts of lag — so the second read returned an older state than the first. Nothing was deleted; the user just travelled backwards.
exercises.goDeeper: The fix is to pin each user to one replica — say by hashing their user id — so every read comes from the same copy. That copy may be stale, but it will never go backwards. Consistently stale is far less alarming to a human than flickering.

exercises.prompt: When is replication lag at its worst?
choices: Exactly when write load is heaviest — the busiest moment, with the most people watching
exercises.why: Lag grows when the leader produces changes faster than followers can apply them. Peak write traffic is precisely when that happens.
exercises.goDeeper: That's the cruel part: your staleness window is widest exactly when the most users are looking. A system that looks perfectly in sync in testing can be seconds behind during a spike — which is also when a support ticket becomes ten thousand support tickets.

exercises.prompt: Which of these genuinely help with replication lag problems? Select all.
choices: Route a user's reads to the leader right after they write
Pin each user to a single replica
Monitor lag and pull badly-lagging replicas out of rotation
exercises.why: Routing, pinning, and monitoring all attack the problem. Adding followers doesn't: each new follower must apply the very same stream of writes, so it lags too — and it adds load to the leader that's shipping to it.
exercises.goDeeper: That last point catches people out. 'We're stale, add replicas' is the wrong reflex — you've added more copies of the staleness, not less of it. Lag is a function of write throughput versus apply speed, and more followers changes neither.

exercises.prompt: You read from an asynchronous follower. What are you actually getting?
choices: A guarantee the data is current
An answer that's correct as of some moment in the past — possibly right now, possibly seconds ago
An error if it's out of date
exercises.why: A follower always gives you a real, valid state of the database — just not necessarily the latest one. It's a photograph, not a live feed.
exercises.goDeeper: That distinction matters: a stale read isn't corrupt or wrong, it's late. Which means the design question is never 'is this allowed to be wrong?' but 'how old is too old for this screen?' — a question the product usually answers better than the engineer.

exercises.prompt: Your leader dies and you promote a follower. With ASYNCHRONOUS replication, what might be lost?
choices: Any writes the leader had already acknowledged but not yet shipped — those are simply gone
exercises.why: Asynchronous means the leader said 'done' before followers had the change. If it dies in that window, those acknowledged writes die with it.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the under-appreciated asterisk in most setups: surviving a crash OF that machine is not the same as surviving the LOSS of that machine. Async replication is fast because it doesn't wait — and 'doesn't wait' is exactly what you're relying on not to matter at the worst possible moment.

exercises.prompt: The leader isn't actually dead — it's just unreachable for 30 seconds. You promote a follower. Then the old leader comes back, still believing it's the leader. What now?
choices: Split brain: two leaders both accepting writes, producing conflicting data with no arbiter
exercises.why: Two nodes both convinced they're in charge, both taking writes. Now you have two divergent versions of the truth and no principled way to merge them.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why failover systems use fencing — forcibly locking the old leader out (sometimes by literally cutting its power) before promoting anyone. The reason it's necessary is uncomfortable: from the outside you genuinely cannot distinguish 'dead' from 'slow.' You can only pick a timeout and accept being wrong sometimes.

exercises.prompt: So how should you set the failover timeout?
choices: As short as possible — recover fast
As long as possible — never risk a false promotion
You're choosing which mistake to make: too short promotes during a harmless blip (risking split brain), too long leaves you down during a real failure
exercises.why: There's no setting that's right in both directions, because the question 'is it dead or just slow?' has no answer from outside. You're picking which way you'd rather be wrong.
exercises.goDeeper: Get comfortable with this shape — it recurs constantly in distributed systems. When a decision is genuinely undecidable, engineering stops being about finding the right answer and starts being about choosing your failure mode deliberately, rather than discovering it during an incident.

exercises.prompt: A financial ledger, where a write you've acknowledged must never be lost. Slide toward your replication mode.
exercises.why: If losing an acknowledged write is unacceptable, the write has to exist on a second machine before you say 'done.' That's what synchronous means, and there's no way to have the guarantee without the wait.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice you didn't get to have both. Either the write waits for a second machine or it doesn't — that's networks and physics, not a setting someone forgot to optimize. Anyone promising you both is selling you an async system with a confident voice.

exercises.prompt: Why not just let two datacenters each run a leader that accepts writes?
choices: You can — but now two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same row, and you must decide how to resolve those conflicts
Only one datacenter can hold data
exercises.why: Multi-leader buys write availability and local latency in each region, and pays for it with conflicts — the exact problem single-leader was designed to avoid.
exercises.goDeeper: Which is why multi-leader stays rare for a single source of truth, and shows up where conflicts are naturally rare or genuinely resolvable: data partitioned per region, or collaborative editing where merging two edits is a solved problem rather than a coin flip.

exercises.prompt: Users report that data they just saved disappears — but only during peak hours. Setup: writes go to the leader, reads are load-balanced across 3 async followers. Diagnosis?
choices: Replication lag under peak write load — reads are landing on followers that are behind. Route reads to the leader for a window after a user writes
exercises.why: Peak write load widens the lag window, so a read right after a write is likely to hit a follower that hasn't applied it yet. Nothing is lost — the follower is just answering from the past.
exercises.goDeeper: The 'only during peak hours' detail is the tell, and it's worth learning to hear. A bug that appears only under load is usually a timing window that's always been there, finally grown wide enough to be visible.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of replication?
choices: Replicas make you faster and safer, for free
Copies buy read capacity and survival, and charge you in lag, in writes lost on async failover, and in the risk of split brain
exercises.why: Real benefits, real bill. Each cost is a direct consequence of the copy existing at all — not a defect you can engineer away.
exercises.goDeeper: Unit 5 said every copy costs you a consistency question. Replication is that bill, itemized: lag is the question while the copy is catching up, failover is the question at the worst possible moment, and split brain is the question with two confident answers.
